summary:
Espirito Santo sits within Brazil's national framework for LGBTI rights; the national record carries the marriage, identity-marker and hate-crime provisions that apply here, and what follows is the state's own layer of law, institutions and enforcement.

Facilities are contested at municipal level. On 6 June 2022 the Vitoria City Council approved a bill banning the installation of unisex restrooms in the city. The source records the council vote but not whether the mayor signed or vetoed the measure, so its current legal force is unresolved.

On 14 April 2024 the Legislative Assembly of Espirito Santo approved a bill restricting athletes' participation in competitions according to biological sex. Governor Renato Casagrande vetoed it on 28 April 2024.

On 21 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly approved a law allowing parents to prohibit their children from participating in classes dealing with LGBTQ topics. LGBTQ rights organisations challenged it at the Supreme Federal Court, which began hearing the case on 21 November 2025 and struck the law down in May 2026 by 8 votes to 2; Justice Carmen Lucia stated that it violated the Brazilian Constitution.

Partner recognition was addressed in Espirito Santo before the national framework was settled. On 3 August 2012 a judge in Colatina authorised registration of the marriage of Ediana Calixto and Kamila Roccon, the first same-sex marriage recognised in the state. The State Public Prosecutor's Office appealed and the recognition was revoked on 15 August; on 20 September the state Court of Justice reversed that decision and authorised recognition. On 15 August 2012 the General Inspectorate of Justice issued a Circular Letter requiring all civil registries to treat same-sex marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples, making Espirito Santo the third Brazilian state to address the question statewide.

State institutions have also acted on document recognition. On 22 January 2025 the Public Defender's Office of Espirito Santo filed suit to secure name and gender rectification for a non-binary person from Vitoria, and the court granted the request and authorised the rectification. On 27 June 2025 the Legislative Assembly and the Public Defender's Office held a free event to help trans, non-binary and travesti people change their name and gender on official documents.
tangentialFactors:
Restriction attempts in the state have concentrated on facilities, sport and schooling rather than on criminal law, and none of the measures passed in the current cycle took effect as written. The April 2024 athlete-eligibility bill was vetoed by Governor Renato Casagrande, and the June 2025 school-content law was struck down by the Supreme Federal Court.

Education restriction has a longer local history. In 2015 the municipality of Cachoeiro de Itapemirim passed a law prohibiting ideological indoctrination in city schools, a decade before the assembly passed its own school-content measure.

The state's own protection machinery runs through its courts and public defender's office rather than through the legislature: the January 2025 rectification suit for a non-binary resident of Vitoria was granted by a state court, and the state was the third in the country to direct its civil registries statewide on marriage recognition in 2012.
localsOnly:
For residents, the practical points of contact with the legal system are document rectification and school policy. Name and gender changes on official documents can be pursued through the Public Defender's Office and through periodic Legislative Assembly events, most recently on 27 June 2025, which was open to trans, non-binary and travesti people.

Marriage registration practice was standardised for the state's registries by the General Inspectorate of Justice Circular Letter of 15 August 2012, which required civil registries to treat same-sex marriages on the same terms as opposite-sex couples.

School content remains contested at local level: the 2025 parental opt-out law passed by the Legislative Assembly was struck down in May 2026, and the 2015 Cachoeiro de Itapemirim ideological-indoctrination law remains part of the municipal record. No Espirito Santo-specific count of anti-trans violence or of hate-crime enforcement appears in the sources, so residents' risk cannot be measured against the state's general crime picture.
outOfScopeNotes:
The current status of the Vitoria unisex-restroom bill approved on 6 June 2022 is unresolved in the sources: the mayor's signature or veto is not recorded, and no later confirmation of its effect was available.

Whether the veto of the April 2024 athlete-eligibility bill was sustained or overridden is not recorded.

No state-level data on anti-trans violence, killings or hate-crime prosecutions in Espirito Santo appears in the source inventory, so no rate for the state can be stated and no comparison with the national figures can be made.

The general claim that larger cities offer more legal infrastructure while smaller cities and rural areas carry more social friction is not sourced at state level for Espirito Santo and is not treated here as a finding about this state.
